## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why2: Every option is in my trade's words (guests, the desk, forwarding unanswered calls, the hotel's voice), and the title is a single clear question.
screens.why3: I know from the pilots which step makes reservation teams hesitate, and it is handing guests to an AI that speaks as the hotel.
screens.why4: The three efforts are distinct and in my words, but 'Set which calls the AI hands to the desk' is a setup step we mostly do with the director, not something an agent would balk at, and no option covers a data protection or works council sign-off that German agents would raise.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most would let an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice' is my adoption-friction point word for word, with nothing reworded.

screens.why1: Choosing whether to ask for a pilot fits right before the study goes out, after the problem and solution are set.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is my own word, since my whole offer is a pilot, and the hint shows exactly the line people will see.
screens.why3: I know whether I want pilots, because a pilot at one location is how I sell.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the complete choice here, and the two options are distinct.
screens.why5: My pilot is a paid one: €3,000 up front, money-back, at one hotel. This line asks for a free email, and it would go to reservation agents who cannot sign for it, so it drifts from my offer.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Yes: 'Would your hotel try a money-back pilot at one location? Leave your email and we'll pass it to your reservations director.' / No pilot

screens.why1: Picking who asks my questions belongs right before the study goes out to reservation agents, after the pilot offer is settled.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, typing, credits and text messages into one block, and it calls the pick a voice while the interviewer is on video with a face, so I would read it twice.
screens.why3: I know my agents and how they would take a call from an interviewer, so I can judge which voice suits them.
screens.why4: Two names with a 5-second sample are distinct and enough, but nothing says whether Daphne or Saskia asks in German, which is the first thing I need to know for agents in Munich and Berlin.
screens.why5: It still says reservation agents, and nothing of Codyco or the AI receptionist leaks into who asks.

screens.why1: Having chosen who asks the questions, choosing how reservation agents answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'Daphne Daphne' reads as a duplicated name and 'Hear her' / 'Still recording' run into the option text, so I need a second read to separate the label from its status.
screens.why3: I know my agents answer between calls on a busy desk, so I can judge whether they'd rather tap or talk.
screens.why4: AI voice, text, and let-them-choose cover the real choices, are distinct, and each carries its readiness.
screens.why5: It names my respondents as reservation agents and leaks nothing of Codyco's product or the director's role.
screens.instead: How should reservation agents answer? -- Daphne asks aloud on video, they talk, type or tap (ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap, speaking or typing into boxes (ready now) / Let them choose when they open the link (ready when Daphne is)

screens.why1: After choosing how reservation agents answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen, but the option explains itself.
screens.why3: I know which hotel groups and reservation offices I can reach by name, so I can answer this myself.
screens.why4: Three distinct ways to reach people (my own contacts, a Keel search, an open link in a group), covering the real choices.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks; it is a neutral sending choice.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" is plain, but the number beside it, "3 holding · 7 people answered", reads as 3 of my 7 hotel people rather than 3 of 3 beliefs, and it doesn't say the verdict rests on relative advantage sitting exactly at the bar.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, but each card says what was counted, over how many (of 7) and where the bar sits (5 of 7), so I can read all three at once.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry my three beliefs word for word, though the statement above them is garbled ("the reservation agent the hotel forwards calls nobody picks up to the AI reservation agent") and wouldn't survive being shown to a hotel group.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next: not that the money case only just held, not to make the €3,000 pilot pitch about recovered bookings, and not to settle the conditions three agents put on letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, but "Holding up" sits flat over a relative-advantage result exactly at the bar (5 of 7, one person from failing) and an adoption result where 3 of the 6 yeses are conditional, so the page sounds firmer than seven reservation agents can carry.
screens.instead: Holding, just: all 3 beliefs held with 7 agents, but whether missed calls become bookings is exactly at the bar (5 of 7) and 3 of 6 would let the AI answer only on a condition; find out those conditions before pitching the €3,000 pilot.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against with my bar marked at 5, all readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "unanswered calls could be forwarded to another number" are word for word what I checked, though the Asked line ("Did forward unanswer calls...") is garbled and asks what they did rather than what they could do.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me forwarding is not the blocker and points me to adoption friction as the one to watch, which is a concrete next place to look.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and flagged as "a lean, not a call", but "is not what will stop them" is said flatly from seven people while Aylin's quote shows an old desk-only phone system and an owner who won't pay to replace it.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 can forward missed calls, a lean from 7 people; one desk is on a phone system that can't forward without IT and an owner who won't pay, so plan a setup path for older systems and look at adoption friction next.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 said it would have gone better · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I know my belief held and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts better / same / worse over 7 people, with 5 better (all a lot), 1 same and 1 worse, and the strip puts the marker at my bar of 5. All three are plain on first look, though "Better · 5 5 a lot" is a little crowded.
screens.why_b3: The card is "Relative advantage" and the belief is my line word for word, "missed calls turned into bookings", as I checked it on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the 5 of 7 and points me to Adoption friction, but it never says that I passed with no margin, or what the two against (call center already covers nights; guests want a person) mean for whom I sell to.
screens.why_b5: It says "at the bar", not strong, shows 7 answered, calls it "a lean, not a call" and flags that the answer is a hypothetical, so nothing overclaims.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only just: one more 'no difference' and it fails. The two against are a group whose call center already answers after six and a desk that won't hand guests to a machine, so lead with groups that have no after-hours cover.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7", so I see at once that my belief held and by how much it cleared the bar.
screens.why_b2: The four answer bars show 3 Yes, 3 Yes-if-worth-it, 0 Probably not and 1 No over 7 people, and the strip puts 6 for against the marker at 5, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Adoption friction and says "Most would let an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice", word for word the belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line says what would make it worth it to the 3 conditional agents "is below", but below there are only names and "Yes, if it was clearly worth it", so I don't learn which proof (bookings recovered, call quality, the hotel's own greeting) to lead the pilot with.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n=7 visible, splits 3 as-is from 3 on a condition, and calls the result "a small group: a lean, not a call", so it doesn't oversell a result where half of the support is conditional.
screens.instead: 3 of 7 would let it answer as is and 3 would if it proved itself -- Murat, Chiara and Aylin each want to see [their condition] first, so make that the first thing the pilot shows; Tobias won't hand guests to an AI at all.

screens.why_b1: Each box states the verdict with its number right beside it ('Compatibility held, 6 of 7'; 'Relative advantage held, 5 of 7' with 'at the bar' on the status line), and they agree with the cards I already read.
screens.why_b3: Both dimension names and both belief lines are word for word the ones I checked on the way in: forwarding unanswered calls, and missed calls turned into bookings.
screens.why_b4: The screen says nothing about what to do. It doesn't flag that relative advantage sits exactly at the bar, or that groups whose call center already covers after hours are a weaker segment for me, or that old phone systems that can't forward need an IT path in onboarding.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, but 'the 1 who said no' heads Aylin's answer, which was 'Only sometimes', and 'the 2 who said no' covers a 'No difference'. That is a soft relabelling of what they said, and a belief held only at the bar is still just called 'held'.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I didn't type: the owner won't pay to replace a phone system that can't forward, a group whose call center covers after six has its pain in group requests and emails rather than calls, and a desk that won't hand guests to a machine 'even if it sounds like us'.
screens.instead: Relative advantage held only at the bar, 5 of 7: groups whose call center covers after hours see no difference, so lead with groups without one, and plan an IT path for phone systems that can't forward. Also show Adoption friction's 3 conditional yeses and what they asked for.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks that I am the right person before anything else, which is the obvious place for it.
screens.why2: Hotel group, central reservations and call center are everyday words in my office in Munich, and I can answer it on the first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly where I work and that our group runs a central reservations office, so I can answer it without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly for a gate, and per the rules a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It repeats the founder's segment almost word for word and gives away nothing about any product or plan.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options that are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Do you work at a hotel group in Germany that runs a central reservations office or call center, taking booking calls? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: As the gate after the screener it makes sense to check I've actually taken booking calls lately before asking me about one, though on a trade-fair Saturday in Munich the answer is so obviously yes that it hardly sorts anyone out.
screens.why2: Booking call, shift, last 7 days: those are the words I use every day, and I'd answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: Whether calls came in on my shift is the most basic thing I know about my week.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct, but a gate should have no escape at all, and here there are two: 'I can't recall one particular booking call' is odd when I take dozens a shift, and 'I'd rather not say' is not supposed to exist.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's point is the calls that don't get answered, and asking only whether a call came in drifts from that toward a question nearly every agent passes.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'Yes or no' is easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call ring out or drop before anyone on your team could take it? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after I said calls came in on my shift, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are words I use every day at the reservations office, and the rest is plain, though 'hands a call to the desk by rules the hotel sets' is a bit stiff.
screens.why3: Calls nobody picks up on a trade-fair Saturday, taking payment and getting the booking into the PMS is exactly my day.
screens.why4: A card to read, no options.
screens.why5: It talks about 'your hotel' forwarding calls when I sit in a central reservations office, and calling the product an 'AI reservation agent' borrows my own job title, which drifts a little.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is long; 'the PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo' sounds like four different things rather than examples, and the belief line repeats the how instead of pointing back to it.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent. Calls nobody in your office picks up go to it; it answers like your hotel, takes the payment and puts the booking straight into your PMS, such as OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo, and passes a call to a person by your rules. The people building it believe this would catch the calls you miss.

screens.why1: Asking whether Codyco would fit how I handle calls makes sense right after the idea card, but jumping straight to call forwarding without saying what it has to do with Codyco is abrupt.
screens.why2: "Did forward unanswer calls to another number?" has no subject and a broken word, so I can't tell if it asks whether I forwarded calls, whether our system did, or whether I could have Codyco take them.
screens.why3: I know whether our office forwards unanswered calls to an overflow line or another hotel, but our phone system does that, not me on one call, so I'd be guessing what "my last booking call" has to do with it.
screens.why4: Yes, easily and Yes, most of the time answer "could you" or "how often", not "did it happen on one call", so the true answer, yes it went to overflow or no it was picked up, isn't cleanly there.
screens.why5: The founder must have meant something like "could you have unanswered calls forward to another number", so Codyco could pick them up, but the garbled stem has lost that meaning and reads as a broken machine fill.
screens.why6: Heard once, "Did forward unanswer calls to another number?" sounds like a mistake, and I'd ask the agent to repeat it instead of answering.
screens.instead: Think of the booking calls nobody picks up at your office. Could you have them forwarded to another number? I'll read three options: Yes; yes, with some steps; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: After asking whether my last call fits Codyco, asking whether it would have made that call go better is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but 'go better for you' is vague: I took that call myself, so does it mean easier for me, better for the guest, or a booking that otherwise wouldn't happen?
screens.why3: My last booking call is one I answered and booked myself on a busy fair Saturday, so whether an AI agent would have done it better is a guess; the calls it would really help are the ones nobody picked up.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse, plus I can't tell, covers every answer I could give, with no overlap.
screens.why5: The card names it an AI reservation agent on purpose, and the question stays on the founder's point of handling booking calls without leaking anything else.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options I can hold after one hearing, and one escape at the end.
screens.instead: Think of the last booking call on your shift that nobody could pick up. Would Codyco have turned it into a booking, or not? Yes, it would have booked it · Maybe, if the guest stayed on · No, the guest needed a person · Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: After the idea card and asking whether it would have helped my last call, asking whether I'd let it take guests is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "In your hotel's voice" makes me stop: do they mean an AI that sounds like us on the phone, or one that speaks for the hotel under its name?
screens.why3: Whether an AI answers our guests is decided by revenue and the head of reservations, not by me on the phones, so I'd be guessing at what I'd want rather than what I'd do.
screens.why4: Yes, a conditional yes, probably not and no cover what I'd say, they don't overlap, and "I can't tell" fits someone who isn't sure.
screens.why5: It stays with the idea card, an AI that answers our callers, and nothing else of the product or the founder's own terms comes through.
screens.why6: It's short, it's one question, and four short options plus the escape are easy to hold after hearing them once.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, it would answer calls for your hotel under its name. Would you be okay with that, or not? Yes · Yes, if it was clearly worth it · Probably not · No · I can't tell
